summary: Describes the registration policies for the .gov top-level domain used by U.S. government organizations. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1816.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for who gets a .gov address, the way the Internet marks U.S. government websites.

subtitle: The registration policies and eligibility rules for the .gov top-level domain.

tldr.problem: U.S. government organizations were registering .gov domains with no guidance, resulting in multiple registrations per agency and naming schemes that confused the public.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC establishes clear rules based on the official FIPS 95-1 list of U.S. government agencies: only top-level agencies, independent agencies, and autonomous law enforcement components are eligible for direct .gov registrations, with one registration per agency.
tldr.outcome: This policy was replaced by RFC 1816 as domain practices continued to evolve, but it established the principle that .gov registrations should reflect official government structure.

today: RFC 1811 is obsolete and replaced by RFC 1816. However, it established the foundational principle that .gov is reserved for U.S. federal government organizations and should reflect the official structure of government.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The .gov top-level domain is delegated to the U.S. Federal Networking Council for use only by federal government entities. Before this RFC, federal agencies were registering domains freely with no standard, leading to confusion and unnecessary registrations.

RFC 1811 establishes a registration policy based on FIPS 95-1, the official government standard that lists all U.S. federal agencies. This ensures domain names match the real structure of government and people can find agencies easily.
sections.plainLanguage: The government decided that .gov addresses should follow how the government is actually organized, using an official list of all the agencies.

sections.title: Eligibility and Rules
sections.content:
Top-level entities (like the Department of Agriculture), independent agencies, and autonomous law enforcement components (such as the FBI and Secret Service) are eligible for registration directly under .gov. Subsidiary components are not eligible for separate registrations.

The RFC allows an exception for cross-agency collaborative organizations with chartering documents. However, state and local government entities must register under .us, not .gov, and Defense Department organizations must use .mil. Organizations that already had multiple .gov registrations were given three years to consolidate to a single primary domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Big agencies and independent parts like the FBI can get their own .gov address. But pieces inside an agency do not get separate ones, and state governments use .us instead.

sections.title: Implementation and Transition
sections.content:
The RFC required that domain names be derived from the official agency name in FIPS 95-1, such as USDA.gov or Agriculture.gov. The .gov registration authority would assign new registrations on a first-come, first-served basis.

Agencies with multiple existing registrations had six months to select a primary domain, with secondary domains ceasing to accept new delegations. After one year, secondary domains would be undelegated, and after three years, all registrations would be deleted unless mirrored in the primary domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Each agency picks one main web address based on its official name. If agencies had more than one before, they had a few years to clean that up.

references.text: "Codes for the Identification of Feral and Federally Assisted Organizations", FIPS PUB 95-1, January 1993.
Postel, J., "Domain Name System Structure and Delegation", RFC 1591, March 1994.
